title: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite
content:
sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite

This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025. It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics.

Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO. In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck.

sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy!

It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync:

The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most.

Update: Hah! Turns out I wrote about this application of sqlite_rsync back in October 2024 when the tool was first released.

title: Ansible Fails waiting for privilege escalation on Ubuntu 26
content:
I've slowly been moving my servers from Ubuntu 22 and 24 to 26 this year, and noticed my Ansible automation starts failing if I have password protection for sudo use:

$ ansible-playbook main.yml -K
BECOME password: 

PLAY [Security] *******************************************************

TASK [Gathering Facts] ***********************************************************************
fatal: [my-server.local]: FAILED! => 
 msg: 'Timeout (12s) waiting for privilege escalation prompt: '

Apparently Ubuntu's been rewriting system utilities in Rust, and the sudo-rs version that ships on Ubuntu 26.04 has some incompatiblities with the sudo I've used on servers for 20+ years.

title: Electrek Speculates on Trump’s Claim He ‘Protected’ Elon Musk After a ‘Very Tough Incident’ During His First Term
content:
Fred Lambert, writing for Electrek:

On August 7, 2018, Musk tweeted that he was “considering taking Tesla private at $420. Funding secured.” It wasn’t. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had shown interest, but no deal or price had been agreed, and the take-private plan was dead within three weeks.

The SEC sued Musk for securities fraud on September 27, 2018. The agency didn’t only ask for a fine. It asked the court to bar Musk from serving as an officer or director of any public company. That would have meant no more Elon at Tesla, which lines up with “you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me” better than anything else on this list.

And then it went away fast. Two days later, the SEC announced a settlement: Musk stayed CEO, gave up the chairman title for three years, and he and Tesla each paid $20 million, $40 million in total. Tesla added two independent directors and agreed to have a lawyer pre-approve Musk’s material tweets, but the SEC never fully enforced it. Musk didn’t admit or deny anything.

The SEC was run at the time by Jay Clayton, a Trump appointee.

I’ll bet that’s what Trump was referring to. Like most of Trump’s corrupt acts, it happened right in the open.

 ★

title: Why did it seem that the entries in the CoreApplication Properties expired when the source application shut down?
content:
Last time, we confirmed that entries in the Core­Application.Properties are not tied to the lifetime of the apartment that added them. But Luca claimed that they did. Where did this claim come from?

While it’s true that the entries don’t expire, the objects might expire.

If the object you put into the Core­Application.Properties are not agile, then they must be used in the apartment that created them, and therefore when that apartment shuts down, the objects become unusable.

When you put a non-agile object in the Core­Application.Properties, it says, “Oh no, this object is not agile. I need to create an agile wrapper for it, and put the wrapper in the Properties collection.” It has to do this because the Properties is a global object that can be used from any thread, so it’s possible to retrieve the object from a thread different from the one that the non-agile object belongs to.

When you retrieve the object from the Properties, the Core­Application unwraps the agile wrapper, and if you aren’t on the same thread that the wrapped object belongs to, then the COM infrastructure will create a proxy for the wrapped object. When you call methods on the proxy, the COM infrastructure switches to the object’s original thread, calls the method, and then takes the results back to the calling thread, possibly creating proxies for them if those results are themselves non-agile.

This agile wrapper is nothing special. It’s the standard agile wrapper created by Ro­Get­Agile­Reference function.

Here are some of the more common libraries for implementing COM objects and whether their objects are agile.

Library Object agility
C# Agile
C++/WinRT default Agile
C++/WinRT + non_agile Non-agile
WRL default Agile
WRL + __WRL_CONFIGURATION_LEGACY__ Non-agile
C++/CX default Agile
C++/CX + [MarshalingBehavior(Standard)] Non-agile
Handwritten Agile if you aggregate the
free-threaded marshaler

My guess is that Luca implemented a COM object by hand, since the other libraries require you to opt out of agility explicitly, in which case the lack of agility probably would have been called out.

Okay, so now we understand how Luca came to the conclusion that entries in the Core­Application.Properties are auto-removed when the source apartment shuts down: The tests were done with non-agile objects. What they observed was the value expiring, not the entry.

Next time, we’ll look some more at what happens when you put non-agile objects in the Core­Application.Properties.

The post Why did it seem that the entries in the CoreApplication Properties expired when the source application shut down? appeared first on The Old New Thing.
